Significance tests

A coin shows heads 33 times in 50 tosses. Is it biased, or was it chance? In a study a drug cures 72 out of 100 patients, the old one only 60%. Does it really work better? A significance test makes such decisions by a fixed rule and tells you exactly how often you will be wrong.

8 LESSONS2 UNITSDECIDING UNDER UNCERTAINTY
WHAT YOU WILL LEARN IN THIS CHAPTER
  • formulate the null hypothesis and the alternative hypothesis, fix the test statistic and the significance level
  • find the rejection region and the critical value and set up a decision rule
  • carry out one-tailed and two-tailed tests, also with a CAS
  • tell type I and type II errors apart and interpret them

UNIT 14 LESSONS

1Hypotheses, rejection region, decision rule

We first assume that the coin is fair: $p = 0.5$. Under this assumption $X$, the number of heads in 50 tosses, is binomially distributed with $n = 50$ and $p = 0.5$. Very large values are then rare: $P(X \ge 32) \approx 0.032$, $P(X \ge 31) \approx 0.059$.

We decide: if 32 or more heads come up, we no longer believe in a fair coin. We would then wrongly suspect a fair coin in only about 3.2% of cases. You fix this boundary before you toss.

KEY POINT · SIGNIFICANCE TEST

Null hypothesis $H_0\colon p = p_0$ (the status quo), alternative hypothesis $H_1$, for example $p > p_0$ (right-tailed) or $p < p_0$ (left-tailed).

Test statistic $X$: number of hits in the sample, under $H_0$ binomially distributed with $n$ and $p_0$. Significance level $\alpha$, usually 5%.

Rejection region $\overline{A}$: the extreme values that together have at most the probability $\alpha$ under $H_0$. Right-tailed $\overline{A} = \{k, \ldots, n\}$ with the smallest $k$ for which $P(X \ge k) \le \alpha$. $k$ is called the critical value.

Decision rule: if the result lies in $\overline{A}$, $H_0$ is rejected: the result is significant. Otherwise $H_0$ is not rejected.

What you want to show belongs in $H_1$. Because only rejecting $H_0$ is a strong statement with a known probability of error.

Not rejected does not mean proved. It only means: the data are not enough to refute $H_0$.

INTERACTIVE · THE SIGNIFICANCE TEST

Set $n$, $p_0$, the type of test and $\alpha$. Red is the rejection region. Move the observed number of hits $k$ and read off the decision.

EXAMPLE 1 · THE NEW DRUG

An old drug cures 60%. The manufacturer of a new one claims it works better. In a study with 100 patients, 72 are cured. Test with $\alpha = 5\%$.

$H_0\colon p = 0.6$, $H_1\colon p > 0.6$, $X \sim B(100, 0.6)$. $P(X \ge 69) \approx 0.040 \le 0.05$, but $P(X \ge 68) \approx 0.062$. So $\overline{A} = \{69, \ldots, 100\}$.

72 lies in the rejection region: $H_0$ is rejected. The better effect is significant at the 5% level.

EXAMPLE 2 · LEFT-TAILED

A party claims to have 40% support. An opponent suspects less and asks 200 people. Find the rejection region for $\alpha = 5\%$.

$H_0\colon p = 0.4$, $H_1\colon p < 0.4$. We need the largest $k$ with $P(X \le k) \le 0.05$: $P(X \le 68) \approx 0.047$. $\overline{A} = \{0, \ldots, 68\}$. Only with 68 or fewer people in favour is the suspicion supported.

EXERCISES

Formulate $H_0$ and $H_1$: a) A supplier guarantees at most 10% rejects, the buyer has doubts. b) A teacher suspects that more than half of the class copies their homework.

a) $H_0\colon p = 0.1$, $H_1\colon p > 0.1$   b) $H_0\colon p = 0.5$, $H_1\colon p > 0.5$

For exercise 1 a): the buyer checks 50 parts. Use the widget to find the rejection region for $\alpha = 5\%$. How does he decide with 7 faulty parts?

$\overline{A} = \{10, \ldots, 50\}$ ($P(X \ge 10) \approx 0.025$, $P(X \ge 9) > 0.05$). With 7, $H_0$ is not rejected.

How does the rejection region of the coin test ($n = 50$, right-tailed) change if you choose $\alpha = 1\%$ instead of $5\%$? What does that mean for the decision with 33 heads?

$\overline{A} = \{34, \ldots, 50\}$ instead of $\{32, \ldots\}$. With 33 heads: significant at the 5% level, but not at the 1% level.

Why should you fix $\alpha$ and the rejection region before you know the data?

Otherwise you can put the boundary where the desired result comes out. The stated probability of error is then no longer correct.

UNIT 24 LESSONS

2Two-tailed tests, type I and type II errors

Is a dice fair? Too many and too few sixes would be suspicious. So you split $\alpha$ between both sides, $\tfrac{\alpha}{2}$ each.

Every decision can be wrong. If you reject $H_0$ although it is true, that is a type I error. Its probability is at most $\alpha$. If you keep $H_0$ although in reality a different $p$ holds, that is a type II error. Its probability $\beta$ depends on the true $p$.

KEY POINT · TWO-TAILED, TYPE I AND TYPE II ERRORS

Two-tailed test $H_0\colon p = p_0$ against $H_1\colon p \neq p_0$: $\overline{A} = \{0, \ldots, l\} \cup \{r, \ldots, n\}$ with the largest $l$ for which $P(X \le l) \le \tfrac{\alpha}{2}$ and the smallest $r$ for which $P(X \ge r) \le \tfrac{\alpha}{2}$.

$H_0$ is true$H_1$ is true
$H_0$ rejectedtype I error (at most $\alpha$)correct
$H_0$ not rejectedcorrecttype II error ($\beta$)

A smaller $\alpha$ makes the type I error rarer, but the type II error more frequent. Only a larger sample size makes both smaller.

In court: $H_0$ = innocent. Type I error: convicting the innocent. Type II error: acquitting the guilty. The first one is deliberately kept small.

In the widget: tick “show type II error” and choose a true $p$. Violet is then the true distribution.

EXAMPLE 3 · THE DICE, TWO-TAILED

A dice is rolled 120 times. Test $H_0\colon p = \tfrac16$ (six) against $H_1\colon p \neq \tfrac16$ with $\alpha = 5\%$.

$2.5\%$ on each side: $P(X \le 11) \approx 0.014$, $P(X \ge 29) \approx 0.022$. $\overline{A} = \{0, \ldots, 11\} \cup \{29, \ldots, 120\}$. So 28 sixes are not yet significant, 8 sixes are.

EXAMPLE 4 · TYPE II ERROR

In the drug test (example 1) the new drug really cures 70%. How likely is it that the test misses this?

Type II error: $H_0$ is not rejected, so $X \le 68$, although $p = 0.7$. $\beta = P(X \le 68) \approx 0.367$. In more than one case in three the improvement would go unnoticed. With $p = 0.75$ it would only be about 7%.

EXERCISES

Describe the type I and the type II error in the context of the drug test.

Type I: you think the new drug is better although it is not better. Type II: you think it is not better although it is better.

A coin is tossed 20 times. Use the widget to find the rejection region for a two-tailed test with $\alpha = 5\%$.

$\overline{A} = \{0, \ldots, 5\} \cup \{15, \ldots, 20\}$, $\approx 2.1\%$ on each side.

For the party from example 2 the true support is 35%. What is the probability that the opponent still cannot support her suspicion?

$\beta = P(X \ge 69)$ with $p = 0.35$, $n = 200$: $\approx 0.585$. The test is too weak for such small differences, you would need more people.

Try it in the widget: how does $\beta$ change in the drug test (true $p = 0.7$) if you increase $n$ from 100 to 200? Explain.

$\beta$ falls clearly (to about 0.1). With more data the distributions become relatively narrower and overlap less, the test separates better.

REVIEW · DEEPEN · CONNECT

A company claims that 20% of its raffle tickets win. You suspect more blanks, that is fewer than 20% winners. Formulate the hypotheses.

$H_0\colon p = 0.2$, $H_1\colon p < 0.2$ (left-tailed).

A coin shows heads 9 times in 10 tosses. Test right-tailed with $\alpha = 5\%$.

$P(X \ge 9) = \tfrac{11}{1024} \approx 0.011$, $P(X \ge 8) \approx 0.055$. $\overline{A} = \{9, 10\}$: $H_0$ is rejected.

Connecting with chapter 1.1 of Year 12: explain why “the result is significant, so $H_0$ is false with 95%” is a wrong statement.

$\alpha$ is $P_{H_0}(\text{rejection})$, a conditional probability given that $H_0$ holds. The statement confuses it with $P_{\text{rejection}}(H_0 \text{ false})$, as with the positive rapid test $P_D(+)$ and $P_+(D)$.

EXCURSIONTHE MOST FAMOUS TEST IN STATISTICS

The lady tasting tea

In his book on the design of experiments, the English statistician Ronald A. Fisher tells of a lady who claimed she could tell by the taste whether the milk or the tea had been poured into the cup first.

Fisher planned the test like this: eight cups, four of each kind, in random order. The lady is to pick out the four cups “milk first”. If she is only guessing, there are $\binom84 = 70$ equally likely choices, so all four correct only with probability $\tfrac{1}{70} \approx 1.4\%$. If she succeeds, you reject the null hypothesis “she is only guessing”. Fisher turned this into the basic pattern of every significance test.

Source: Ronald A. Fisher: The Design of Experiments. Oliver and Boyd, Edinburgh 1935, chapter 2.

LOOKING BACKTHE ESSENTIALS AT A GLANCE

HYPOTHESES

$H_0\colon p = p_0$, what you want to show goes in $H_1$.

Drug: $H_1\colon p > 0.6$

REJECTION REGION

Extreme values with probability at most $\alpha$ under $H_0$.

Coin $n = 50$: $\{32, \ldots, 50\}$

TWO-TAILED

$\tfrac{\alpha}{2}$ on each side.

Dice $n = 120$: $\{0, \ldots, 11\} \cup \{29, \ldots, 120\}$

TYPE I AND TYPE II ERRORS

Type I: $H_0$ wrongly rejected ($\le \alpha$). Type II: $H_0$ wrongly kept ($\beta$).

Drug, true $p = 0.7$: $\beta \approx 0.37$
